meta.title: How Does Fox News Frame the WNBA?
meta.description: Analyzing the right-wing politicization of the Women’s National Basketball Association
meta.hed: How Does Fox News Frame the WNBA?
meta.dek: Analyzing the right-wing politicization of the Women’s National Basketball Association
meta.headerImg: wnba-framed.png | The WNBA logo hung inside an empty gilt picture frame

content.value: I’ve loved and played (mediocre) basketball all my life, but I only became a real WNBA fan when I moved to Seattle five years ago. (Let’s go, Storm.) Since then, I’ve also become fixated on a question. Why is Fox News obsessed with the WNBA?

fox-iran-wnba.png | Fox News homepage navigation listing its Hot Topics: War With Iran, then WNBA Controversy | A screenshot from the Fox News home page in August 2026. Their hottest topics: literal war and women’s basketball.
This question dawned on me slowly, especially since I don’t read or watch Fox News myself.

The first clue came at a family gathering. I was chatting with an older conservative family member, who, out of the blue, started name-dropping WNBA players, saying praiseworthy things about superstar Caitlin Clark and suspect things about other Black players.
This person has never seen a WNBA game in their life. But they do mainline Fox News on cable TV.

value.caption: Fox News clips from Riley Gaines on Hannity, The Will Cain Show, and Clay Travis on The Ingraham Angle.

content.value: The second clue: my web browser. As I started reading more WNBA news, my Google Chrome app recommended more WNBA news. That made sense. But then I started getting served coverage from, of all places, Fox News. Wait… what?
I saw dozens of Fox News takes on women’s basketball, often with a clear political bias, and an implicitly racist and homophobic framing.

clips: June 2026 | pink | Who is Alyssa Thomas? ((Alyssa Thomas|face))WNBA star suspended for punching Caitlin Clark ((Caitlin Clark|face)) in the throat
January 2025 | green | WNBA star ((DiJonai Carrington|face)) who hurt Caitlin Clark's ((Caitlin Clark|face)) eye calls for league to take action against Trump administration policies
May 2025 | pink | Dave Portnoy calls Angel Reese ((Angel Reese|face)) a jacka-- for jealousy of Caitlin Clark ((Caitlin Clark|face)) in response to ESPN analyst

content.value: Headline after headline pit the league’s most famous straight white star, Clark, against other WNBA players, mainly Black and/or queer women, like Alyssa Thomas, DiJonai Carrington, or Angel Reese.

When it comes to sports, there are, at least seemingly, facts. This team won, and this team lost. This player scored a lot of points. You would expect a lot of similar coverage. But these headlines were clearly different.
So I decided to collect some data.  How does Fox News cover the WNBA compared to everybody else?

steps.text: Let’s start with headlines. If all outlets mentioned Caitin Clark equally, she would be here in the middle.
But Fox News mentions Clark 3.2x more than other outlets.
steps.clip: race | July 2026 | pink | CNN's Abby Phillip claims GOP lawmakers back ==Caitlin Clark== exclusively because she is White

steps.text: Here’s where the other players stand.
Fox often pairs Clark with—and against—Angel Reese.
Of players on the Indiana Fever, Clark’s team, Fox highlights white players like Sophie Cunningham up to 7.8x more...
…while covering Black players like Aliyah Boston and Kelsey Mitchell up to 1.3x less.

Even though Boston and Mitchell have been extraordinary on the court.

In 2026, Mitchell broke the WNBA record for most consecutive games with 20+ points.

steps.names: A’ja Wilson, Napheesa Collier, Breanna Stewart
steps.text: Fox News discusses all-stars like Napheesa Collier, Breanna Stewart, and A’ja Wilson approximately 3-5x less than other outlets...

steps.names: DiJonai Carrington, Natasha Cloud, Brittney Griner
steps.text: while talking about DiJonai Carrington, Natasha Cloud, and Brittney Griner as much as 4.9x more.
steps.clip: Sun's ==DiJonai Carrington== sends fiery message to fans after appearing to take swipe at Caitlin Clark.

content.value: Why does Fox News talk about Carrington, Cloud, and Griner so much?
DiJonai Carrington, Natasha Cloud, Brittney Griner

It’s political. These players’ vocal leftist views—on race, gender, Black Lives Matter (BLM) and more—make them a target for conservative coverage of the WNBA, which has long sought to frame the league as both dangerously radical and illegitimate.

For example, Carrington has publicly criticized Clark for not being vocal enough in denouncing her racist and bigoted fans. She has fouled Clark and Cunningham in high-profile ways. And she’s made it clear that she doesn’t like Trump.

clips: Sun's DiJonai Carrington ((DiJonai Carrington|face)) sends fiery message to fans after appearing to take swipe at Caitlin Clark.
Jan 2025 | WNBA star DiJonai Carrington ((DiJonai Carrington|face))  flaunts explicit message on pre-game outfit directed at President Trump
Brittney Griner  ((Brittney Griner|face)) is coming home. Will she stand for the anthem now that she's back in the USA?
WNBA player Natasha Cloud ((Natasha Cloud|face)) calls out Israel on Oct 7 while blaming Republicans for government shutdown

content.value: Cloud’s outspoken activism—for BLM, Gaza, trans rights, and more—has also been a focal point. Meanwhile, Griner was imprisoned in Russia in 2022, making her a consistent subject of news. But she is often criticized for her progressive views, too.
And it’s no coincidence that these are all queer Black women.

steps.text: On TV, Fox talks more about Clark ((Caitlin Clark| face)) and Cunningham ((Sophie Cunningham| face)) than other outlets, too.
This is cable news coverage of the WNBA, via their chyrons—you know, those headlines that appear at the bottom of your screen.
Fox News talks incessantly about hard fouls and hits against Clark. This is a kind of dog whistle, as I will explain later.

steps.text:
For other players, we see nearly the same breakdown as the online coverage.

Carrington ((DiJonai Carrington| face)) and Thomas ((Alyssa Thomas| face)) lean more Fox, while Bueckers ((Paige Bueckers| face)) and Collier ((Napheesa Collier| face)) lean more other outlets.

content.value: In the summer of 2026, the right-wing politicization of the WNBA burst into the mainstream.

In July, Sophie Cunningham ((Sophie Cunningham|face))—Clark’s teammate and on-court “bodyguard”—made anti-trans remarks. While she told ESPN that she “got a lot of negative feedback about me hating trans” and clarified that “I never once said that," she also expressed a desire to “protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men"—using the exact language and hateful agenda items of the anti-trans movement. She later doubled down on those comments.
This inspired right-wing politicians and anti-trans advocates around the world to rally around her, including Vice President J.D. Vance, infamous literary TERF J.K. Rowling, and grifter Jennifer Sey.
vance-cunningham-fox.png | Fox News segment showing Vice President J.D. Vance praising Sophie Cunningham | Vice President J.D. Vance praises Sophie Cunningham on Fox News, August 2026.

Trans women’s participation in the WNBA has become a non-stop Fox News talking point. They’ve spent more than 13 hours (!) discussing the WNBA this summer alone. And it’s worth repeating: no transgender players are even currently in the league.

Even Fox News pundits are confused—and exhausted—by this excessive focus. As commentator Jesse Watters recently said on air: “We have to do this again, really? Someone wore a t-shirt at a WNBA game? This isn’t a news story…. We don’t even cover the NBA. Why are we covering the WNBA?”

How did professional women’s basketball—a league that, for decades, most people didn’t watch or care anything about—transform into a mainstream political lightning rod? Despite the recent attention, it didn’t happen overnight. And the media, especially conservative media, played a key role.
So let’s dive into the data and see how Fox News has framed the WNBA as a hot-button culture war issue—one that was primed, at the right moment, to explode.
Fightin’ Words
It’s not just the amount of attention that Fox devotes to the WNBA that matters. It’s also the language they use.

steps.text:
Here’s how Fox’s vocabulary differs from other outlets when reporting on the WNBA.

This is a method (aptly) called “fightin’ words,” which shows the most distinctive words used by one group vs. another.

steps.words: Caitlin Clark, Sophie Cunningham, Angel Reese, DiJonai Carrington, Breanna Stewart, lynx, liberty, aces
steps.text:
You can see Fox’s outsized focus on Clark, Cunningham, Reese, and Carrington.

And the relative neglect of players like Stewie (Breanna Stewart) or other leading teams (Aces, Liberty).

steps.words: social media, white privilege, hard foul, collective bargaining, biological men, transgender athletes, white house, fever star, points rebounds, free agency
steps.text:
If we look at two-word phrases, we can see Fox’s focus on white privilege, transgender athletes, and biological men; on hard fouls; and on social media.

And its relative neglect of collective bargaining and of actual play (points rebounds).
Search any word.

content.value: What about language around specific players, like Clark?

This is an especially juicy question because there is currently a “fight over Caitlin Clark’s soul,” as University of Washington professor Kate Starbird, a leading misinformation researcher and former WNBA player, put it to me.

When Clark was drafted into the league in the spring of 2024, the WNBA culture war debates really heated up. Some commentators noted that Clark’s background as a straight, white, Midwestern star may play a role in her broad appeal—a point that conservatives and Fox News pundits have rejected.

clark-fever-spurlock.jpg | Caitlin Clark, seen from behind in her white Indiana Fever number 22 jersey, releases a jump shot toward the basket. | Photo by Brian Spurlock/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images

Clark is not a “stable” figure for the conservative or liberal media, Starbird said. She’s previously written about the increasing pressure athletes feel to take political stances, especially from their large social media audiences. “The real risk for internet influencers—a class of celebrities that increasingly includes professional athletes—isn’t ‘falling down rabbit holes,’ but being ‘captured’ and radicalized by their audiences,” Starbird claims. This is a risk for everyone from Clark to Cunningham to Carrington and beyond.
The point is that Clark is often talked about more than she talks, and it’s not totally clear what her legacy will be. Let’s take a closer look at the coverage.

steps.text: This is the same approach applied per player, and broken down by sentence part.
steps.title: What happens to Caitlin Clark

steps.words: target, poke, shove, knock, strike, hit, punch
steps.text:
Here’s what happens to Clark, according to Fox News.

She is poked, targeted, hit, punched, struck, shoved, and knocked down.

They emphasize her rough treatment much more than other outlets.
Clark is a white phenom but also a victim and a target.

content.value: The Fox News-WNBA Expanded Universe

Of course, Clark didn’t become Fox’s WNBA golden child white savior overnight. And their right-wing spin on women’s basketball didn’t start recently. It’s been a long (if evolving) game, with a rotating cast of characters.
To stoke controversy, Fox often stages conflict between individuals in click-bait headlines—either between extreme outside voices and WNBA players, or between the WNBA players themselves.
Let’s look at the web they’re been spinning.

steps.text: Each face is someone Fox News named in a WNBA headline. A line means two of them shared a headline.
Even before Clark entered the league, Fox’s coverage was hyper-political.

steps.focus: Joe Biden, Megan Rapinoe, Sue Bird
steps.text: They linked the players’ 2020 BLM activism with Biden, and point guard Sue Bird (and her then-girlfriend Megan Rapinoe) with Democrats.
steps.headline: Biden praises WNBA champs for social justice activism | Sue Bird, Megan Rapinoe attempt to dial up support for Democrats before Election Day |

steps.text: They set Lebron James against Kelly Loeffler, a former WNBA owner and former senator, who was defeated by Democrat Raphael Warnock—in part thanks to WNBA player advocacy.
steps.headline: LeBron James suggests buying WNBA team from Georgia Sen. Kelly Loeffler after projected loss

steps.text:
In 2022, Brittney Griner became the central focal point, because she was shockingly arrested and imprisoned in Russia.

It was a moment when the WNBA became imbricated with broader national and world politics.
After Griner was freed in a prisoner swap, Fox notably turned to Trump to suggest it was a bad deal, plainly devaluing her life.
steps.headline: Trump: Brittney Griner prisoner swap for 'Merchant of Death'  doesn't seem like a very good trade

steps.text: Then, in 2024, Clark joined the WNBA and fully took the spotlight.
She was often pit against Reese.

steps.focus: Caitlin Clark, Angel Reese, Dave Portnoy
steps.text: And Fox turned to people like Barstool Sports's Dave Portnoy to stoke controversy between them.
steps.headline: Dave Portnoy calls Angel Reese a 'jacka--' for 'jealousy' of Caitlin Clark in response to ESPN analyst

steps.text: Steadily Sophie Cunningham became the second biggest node in the network.
And Fox increasingly platformed anti-trans advocates.
Check out the whole network and the headlines.

content.value: Supposedly (But Not Really) Rejecting “Identity Politics”

Fox vociferously rejects “identity politics” in WNBA coverage—the reference of identity categories like race, gender, or sexuality, and the idea that political issues may be partly influenced by or organized around them.

everything's-racist-fox.png | Laura Ingraham and Clay Travis, founder of OutKick, discussing Clark on Fox News. | In this clip, Laura Ingraham and Clay Travis—the founder of OutKick—discuss a USA Today column that suggested some of Clark’s fans were racist and that fouls against her were being weaponized.

Writing for Fox’s Outkick, Bobby Burack criticized ESPN for being “racial idolaters” in their reporting about Clark. There is a false narrative, he claimed, that Clark is only a star “because America has starved for a straight white girl to save them from a league of largely black LGBTQ women.” He concluded: “ESPN ought to add some diversity to its WNBA commentary—diversity of opinion, that is.”
Here’s the irony. Fox News talks more about race, gender, and identity in the WNBA than any other outlet—and about twice as much as ESPN.
Though Fox News claims that everybody else is talking about racism, they’re the ones talking about it the most, including on TV.

value.note: Cable news chyrons, {period}, from the Internet Archive’s Third Eye.

content.value: Across all the outlets, discussion of race and racial justice peaks in 2020. This is true for Fox, too. And it’s an important moment to return to.

wnba-blm-2020.jpg | Minnesota Lynx players standing with linked arms, wearing “Say Her Name” shirts | Minnesota Lynx players wear “Say Her Name” shirts and link arms in honor of Breonna Taylor before a game in July 2020. Phelan M. Ebenhack/AP
In 2020, WNBA players engaged in highly visible protest in support of BLM. They walked off the court during the national anthem and wore BLM and “Say Her Name” shirts on national television.

clips: July 2020 | green | Sen. Kelly Loeffler, co-owner of Atlanta Dream, ==objects to WNBA's social justice plans==
July 2020 | green | WNBA players ==walk off court during national anthem== ahead of season opener
July 2020 | green | WNBA players call on league to ==stop playing national anthem== before games
August 2020 | green | WNBA team wears shirts with ==Jacob Blake's name==, league postpones games following Kenosha shooting

content.value: They also successfully campaigned for Democrat Raphael Warnock to win a U.S. Senate seat, defeating Atlanta Dream co-owner Kelly Loeffler, who was loudly opposed to players’ activism. It became clear that the WNBA could wield real political power, especially from a leftist, progressive perspective.

All this was frequently covered by Fox, and often framed in implicitly disapproving terms. However, unlike other outlets, Fox News continued to make race a focal point after 2020, especially in relation to “race baiting” and “race bullies” around Clark.

clips: May 2026 | The WNBA won't grow this season if mean girls and race bullies refuse to accept Caitlin Clark
July 2026 | Alveda King slams USA Today columnist for invoking Emmett Till in Caitlin Clark piece: 'Pure race-baiting'
July 2026 | Stacey Dales provides much-needed logic to ESPN's Caitlin Clark coverage, dismantles race-baiter on set
May 2026 | Dakich: sports media has created an ‘industry’ out of complaining about white athletes like Caitlin Clark
May 2025 | Wings' Paige Bueckers laments lack of 'equal coverage' of Black women, talks 'White privilege'

content.value: While LGBTQ+ topics were mentioned less frequently overall, Fox News also discussed them more proportionally than any other outlet—with a notably sharp increase this summer.

content.value: Fox’s obsession with race and with transgender women are not disconnected. In fact, these issues are intimately connected.

By dramatizing the danger posed to Clark, and the reverse white racism she supposedly faces, Fox News riles up their base against the broader WNBA, which includes not only many Black women but many gay and queer women, too. (According to a recent Atlantic article by Jemele Hill, the league is approximately 70 percent Black, and somewhere between 25 to 35 percent queer).

In a further twist, Fox News often highlights white players who conform to traditional conventions of femininity, and denigrates Black players who do not, advancing conceptions of ideal (straight white femme) womanhood.
Drawing these boundaries has only one obvious end: hating women, including trans women.

One particularly powerful narrative has been about fouls. From the moment Clark entered the WNBA until today, conservatives have pushed a story that other players are fouling and purposely targeting her, often suggesting because she is white. This ramped up to the point that in July 2026 a group of Republican politicians literally sent a letter to the WNBA commissioner.
letter.jpeg | Letter from Republicans to the WNBA commissioner | Letter from Republicans to the WNBA commissioner

In the letter, the politicians threatened that "if discrimination or retaliation is occurring and creating a hostile work environment” in the WNBA, then they would call for an “investigation by the Department of Justice, the Department of Labor, or the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission." They warned that the fouls against Clark might violate “federal civil rights laws.”
The Republicans cite, as evidence, the fact that “Clark has been hip-checked, poked in the eye, and struck in the throat during games.”
Who emphasized exactly these points for months and months? Fox News.
Let’s Not Get Played

Fox News has fanned the flames of the WNBA culture war for years. They have denied that race, sexuality, or gender are relevant considerations in the league, yet foregrounded them more than any other outlet. The implicit misogyny—and suspicion of “social justice” and queer communities—laid the groundwork for the right-wing movement to rise up and seize the WNBA as a central issue.

In 2026, a full quarter of Fox’s online WNBA coverage has mentioned trans athletes or issues, far outstripping the other outlets. Many of these articles panic over transgender women playing in the WNBA (even though no transgender women are playing in the WNBA).

value.note: Share of each outlet's 2026 WNBA articles that mention trans athletes or issues.

content.value: As Jesse Watters recently said on air, “Why are we covering the WNBA?” Or, more pointedly, “This is something I don’t care about.” He said the quiet part out loud. Fox News doesn’t actually care about women’s basketball. Right-wing pundits and politicians are using the WNBA to push their own agendas.

Sports are political. They have always been political. Throughout American history, athletes have been able to use their platform to advocate for justice. And players in the WNBA are a great example of that.
jacob-blake.png | Julio Aguilar / Getty Images | Julio Aguilar / Getty Images
But we should be wary of how narratives about the WNBA are being framed by the right-wing media and outside parties who have little to no actual investment in the league.

When I went to my first WNBA game, I was shocked by how inclusive it felt. Black, queer, and POC women were celebrated on and off the court, as well on the jumbotron and in the stands. The dancers were teenaged girls doing sick hip-hop moves in baggy pants. The Storm’s goofy mascot, Doppler, uses they/them pronouns. Fox News-types like to make hell of things like that (and in fact, they have). But the whole vibe was—and is—truly so nice, welcoming, and fun. It is completely different from every other (men’s) professional sporting event I have ever been to.

How the WNBA will handle all of this increased attention—from the mainstream media, politicians, activists, social media trolls, fans, and my conservative relatives—remains uncertain. After seven and a half years, the WNBA commissioner, Cathy Engelbert, recently announced her retirement. The new commissioner has their work cut out for them.

But I know one thing for sure. The version of the WNBA presented by Fox News is not recognizable to me. We need to see this framing for what it is and push back against it, lest we all get played. Let’s not get played.

Data and Methods

Headlines and Articles. I collected any Fox News article (both headline and full text) that mentioned the WNBA or its players over the past six years, while acknowledging that this story goes back much further. This corpus includes coverage from Outkick, now owned by Fox and published on their site.
As a comparison, I collected parallel WNBA coverage from ESPN, USA Today, CBS Sports, The Athletic (owned by the New York Times), and Just Women’s Sports.

TV Chyrons. Additionally, I gathered nine years worth of cable news chyrons from Fox, MSNBC, and CNN, drawing on data from the Internet Archive's Third Eye OCR feed, and inspired by a very cool analysis by Charlie Smart.
Fightin Words. The word comparisons use “fightin’ words” aka weighted log-odds with an informative Dirichlet prior (Monroe, Colaresi & Quinn 2008).
You can find data and code on GitHub.
